newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: No major policy change in new UAE government.
newsitem.headline: No major policy change in new UAE government.

text.p: Gulf oil producer United Arab Emirates on Tuesday announced a reshuffled cabinet with a new petroleum minister but said its oil policy was unchanged.

President Sheikh Zaid bin Sultan al-Nahayan appointed Obaid bin Saif al-Nasseri, a member of a prominent Abu Dhabi family born in 1952, to head the petroleum and mineral resources ministry, the official news agency WAM said.

"UAE oil policy, production and pricing is unchanged," a government official told Reuters. "It is not dependent on individuals and the change of oil minister does not signify in any way an alteration in UAE oil production and pricing policy."
The position of oil minister is not crucial in the UAE, one of the world's wealthiest countries with annual oil income of $9 billion.
It has an OPEC quota of 2.161 million barrels per day and traditionally takes a moderate stance on world oil prices.
It is one of the few oil producers with spare production capacity and sufficient reserves of crude to last a century.
UAE oil policy is determined by the Supreme Petroleum Council chaired by Sheikh Khalifa bin Zaid al-Nahayan, crown prince of Abu Dhabi and heir apparent to Sheikh Zaid, who is in his late 70s.

Analysts said the appointment of Nasseri again showed that UAE oil policy remained firmly in the control of the al-Nahayan family which rules Abu Dhabi, the largest and richest of the seven emirates in the UAE federation.

The new oil minister, who has held a number of senior posts in the financial sector including the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and the National Bank of Abu Dhabi, replaced Rakad bin Salem bin Rakad.
Analysts said Nasseri, like his predecessor, had little experience of the oil industry, but one said "he knows the market and its economics very well".
Rakad, minister of public works and housing, had been acting oil minister since June 1995.

The reshuffle left unchanged the key portfolios of defence, foreign affairs and finance but included a new minister of economy and commerce, Sheikh Fahem bin Sultan al-Qassimi, a former secretary-general of the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council.
Prime Minister Sheikh Maktoum bin Rashid al-Maktoum, ruler of the UAE's second largest emirate Dubai, remained in his post.
"There is no change in policy. It was a restructuring operation," a government official said.

There were eight new faces in the cabinet, including one of the president's younger sons, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zaid al-Nahayan, 24, who was promoted to minister of information and culture. He was previously undersecretary at the ministry.

The UAE was formed in 1971 when Britain withdrew its military protection from the Trucial States -- Abu Dhabi, Ajman, Dubai, Fujairah, Ras al-Khaimah, Sharjah and Umm al-Quwain -- which had subsisted on fishing, pearl diving and trade.
The UAE has no political parties or elected legislature. Sheikh Zaid rules by decree and is the only president the country has ever known.
